I’m having trouble trying to find the right equation to solve what the maximum height is. Alright, I take that it's a word problem? Yeah it is Do you mind explaining the situation? What is the maximum height reached by the ball given the equation y=-16x^2+325.7x+10 Okay, this can be approached in several ways depending on what you've learned so far. (Your request said algebra, so I'm assuming you haven't taken calculus yet) Not to worry though, we have several options. Solving this doesn't necessarily need an equation. I suppose you recognize this function as a quadratic (a parabola). What do you know about the properties of parabolas? Parabolas have a vertex, (which is the highest point) relating to the problem. It also can have x and y intercepts I think. Exactly: what you want to find are the coordinates of the vertex. Notice that the leading coefficient is negative. That tells us that the parabola is curving upwards Downwards* ! Have you learnt the vertex form of the parabola yet? Yeah, when you plug it into dezmos it’s downwards, but I need to find it algebraically I probably have but nothing ever sticks in my brain Not to worry! What the vertex form does for us is make REALLY clear what the coordinates of the vertex are What you currently have looks like this: ax^2 + bx + c So what you're looking for is an equation that looks like this: a * ( x - r )^2 + t And just like that, (r, t) are the coordinates of the vertex! Finding this requires a bit of algebra. So you would plug in the coordinates? Not quite. When we convert the first formula into a formula that looks like the second one, we will automatically find r and t to be those coordinates. So you would have to factor out the equation given? Or?? Yes factoring is how to do it normally There's a really neat shortcut we can use, though. I'm not sure if your teacher wants you to use it... I'll tell you anyway! Yes please r = -b / 2a Then plug in r in the original function to find t. Can you fill those in? Ohh okay okay I got it. I remember that equation. So plugging that into r of the original equation would give me the maximum point? Yes exactly! I get it now Great :) thank you so much No problem! Is there anything else I can help you with? On the board is a short proof of why r = -b/2a in case you haven't seen it before Yeah I see thank you again No problem! See how the 2a cancels to give back the b alone?
